figures.caption: Table 2: Engineered ET features extracted per epoch from the EEGET-ALS dataset. Each feature is z -score normalized per fold using training-set statistics only

Table 3: Parameter configuration and architectural design of the proposed multimodal Siam-ALS network. Both weight-sharing branches use identical parameters across all layers, enforcing the Siamese learning constraint. Notation matches Section 3.2: ei (EEG window), gi (ET features), zi (fused embedding)

Fig. 1: Multimodal synchronization and preprocessing of EEG and ET signals over a 10-second interval. (a) Raw EEG signal overlaid with temporally aligned valid gaze trajectories (horizontal and vertical components). (b) Preprocessed EEG after band-pass filtering (0.5–40 Hz), notch filtering, and resampling, demonstrating improved signal quality and noise reduction. (c) Standardized ET trajectories after removal of invalid samples, capturing normalized gaze dynamics

Fig. 2: EEG and eye-tracking preprocessing pipeline with window-level class balancing between ALS and control. Blue blocks denote the EEG-only processing path; orange blocks denote the ET-only path; both streams converge at the green class-balancing stage, which produces the balanced epoch sets used by all downstream models

Fig. 3: The block diagram of our Siam-ALS framework. Two branches process EEG windows and ET features from subject i and subject j with shared EEG and ET encoders. Fused 64-D embeddings zi and zj are compared via an ℓ1 distance Siamese head, and an embedding-level classifier operates on the learned representation for ALS detection. The detailed configurations of Conv2D, pooling, EEG and ET encoders and MLP are provided in Table 3. (ET and EEG encoders share weights)

Table 6: Leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) validation results for the full Siam-ALS model on EEGET-ALS. Each row reports performance when the listed ALS subject is held out as the sole test-set ALS subject, trained on the remaining five ALS subjects plus a class-balanced control set

Table 7: Clinical performance comparison on EEGET-ALS across all twelve baselines (A1–A12) and the proposed Siam-ALS (A13), reported as mean over 4 subject-level folds. Feature indicates the representation type each model operates on. PPV and NPV are computed on class-balanced test partitions (50% ALS prevalence) and therefore do not reflect clinical prevalence. Sig. reports uncorrected (p < 0.05) significance of AUROC difference from Siam-ALS (Table 10) for the seven directly-tested baselines: ✓ = significantly lower AUROC than Siam-ALS; – = not significant or not tested; Reference = comparison baseline. Explainable indicates whether the model supports attribution over a learned, disease-specific representation

Fig. 5: Clinical performance envelope of Siam-ALS against the full range of twelve baselines (A1–A12) on EEGET-ALS, across seven clinically relevant metrics (Table 7). The dotted inner polygon shows the weakest baseline per metric, the dashed polygon shows the strongest baseline per metric, and the solid indigo polygon shows Siam-ALS. The hatched green region marks where Siam-ALS exceeds the best-performing baseline; on AUROC, Siam-ALS ties the best baselines (A4, A12)

Fig. 6: t-SNE visualisation of embedding spaces on the EEGET-ALS dataset. Left: fused Siam-ALS embeddings learned via metric learning, showing clear separation between ALS and healthy subjects. Middle: EEGNet+ET embeddings with late fusion, where EEG and ET features are combined after separate feature extraction. Right: EEGNet+ET embeddings with mid fusion, where ET features are integrated at an intermediate network layer

Table 9: Architectural ablation on EEGET-ALS comparing five Siamese variants (M0–M4), progressively adding an ET encoder, a fusion encoder, and an embedding-level classifier to a base EEG-only network, trained under an identical protocol (Section 4.2). M4 is architecturally identical to A13 (Table 7) and B3 (Table 8); M2 is comparable to B2, and M0 to B1 (both Table 8); minor numerical differences reflect independent training runs (Section 4.1)

Table 10: Paired t-test and Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparing Siam-ALS AUROC against seven baselines across F = 4 subject-level folds (df = 3 for the t-test). ∆AUROC represents the mean paired difference (Siam-ALS − baseline). Sig. indicates p < 0.05 (uncorrected); no comparison remains significant after Bonferroni correction (α = 0.05/7 ≈ 0.0071). For CNN (A4), one fold had zero AUROC difference and was excluded by the Wilcoxon procedure, leaving n = 3 pairs.

Fig. 7: Training and validation AUROC across epochs for all four cross-validation folds on EEGET-ALS. The model converges within the first few epochs in every fold and maintains consistently high performance (AUROC ≈ 0.99), with closely overlapping training and validation curves, indicating stable learning and good generalization without obvious overfitting

Table 12: Fidelity and cross-method agreement of six explainability methods applied to the Siam-ALS fused embedding. Top-10 AUROC reports mean ± std AUROC retained using only the top-10 ranked embedding dimensions (of 64 total) over 4 folds. Jaccard w/ SHAP reports top-10 dimensional overlap with SHAP, the reference method

Fig. 8: Fidelity comparison of six explainability methods applied to the Siam-ALS fused embedding (Table 12). (a) Mean Top-10 embedding-dimension AUROC per method across 4 folds (error bars: ±1 SD); SHAP attains the highest mean, but all error bars overlap. (b) Rank-ordered fidelity gap relative to SHAP, measured as ∆AUROC@10 (×10−5), showing all six methods cluster within a narrow margin

Fig. 9: SHAP dependence plots for the three top-ranked fused embedding dimensions (E18, E31, E26) on EEGET-ALS. The y-axis shows each dimension’s SHAP contribution to the classifier output in log-odds. Because the final classifier is linear, each relation is exactly linear, with slope equal to the dimension’s logistic-regression coefficient: E18 and E26 push predictions toward ALS, whereas E31 pushes them toward control. Point colour shows the embedding dimension with the strongest interaction, selected automatically by SHAP

Table 15: Explainability scorecard for the seven baselines with paired significance testing against Siam-ALS (Table 10). ∆AUROC and p-value are taken directly from Table 10; Explainable is obtained from Table 7. Models are grouped by uncorrected significance (p < 0.05); no comparison survives Bonferroni correction (α = 0.0071). Across both tiers, explainability rather than accuracy alone is the distinguishing capability of Siam-ALS

Fig. 10: Physiological and embedding-level attribution on EEGET-ALS. (Left) EEG channel×time saliency map (mean absolute gradient) for a representative fused embedding dimension (E52), illustrating how an individual embedding dimension draws on specific EEG channels and time windows. (Right) SHAP beeswarm plot of the 20 highest-ranked fused embedding dimensions; each point is one window, the x-axis shows its SHAP contribution to the log-odds output, and colour indicates the dimension’s value
